context_blurb:
A hurricane is a giant spinning storm born over a warm tropical sea: a wheel of thunderstorms around a calm eye. Its winds are fierce, and the sea it drives ashore can drown a coast. Pilots, buoys and satellites have shown how it works.

A hurricane needs a sea of about 26 degrees Celsius or warmer. When sea water evaporates into water vapour, an invisible gas, it takes in heat, and the vapour carries that heat aloft. High in the storm the vapour condenses, turning back into cloud droplets. Condensing warms the air around it, setting free the heat the vapour held, about 2.5 million joules for every kilogram of water. The warmed air rises faster and draws in more moist sea air, so a hurricane is a heat engine, turning the sea's heat into wind. It runs on the sea's heat, not on sunlight falling on its clouds.

The storm also needs a twist to start it turning. Earth's spin bends moving air to one side, an effect that is zero at the equator and grows toward the poles. Within 5 degrees or so of the equator, Earth's spin barely twists the air, so a hurricane almost never forms there, however warm the sea. The same bend sets which way the storm turns. Northern hurricanes always spin counter-clockwise, and the storms of the south spin clockwise, their mirror image. A draining sink is far too small for Earth's spin to steer, so its swirl can go either way.

In 1943 an Army pilot, Joseph Duckworth, flew a small training plane into a hurricane coming ashore in Texas; no one is known to have flown into one on purpose before. Whether he meant to reach the eye is disputed. Through hammering rain he broke into calm, sunlit air with the ground in sight. The eye is clear because its air sinks, warming and drying as it falls, and sinking air makes no clouds. Around it stands the eyewall, a ring of towering thunderstorms where air rises and the strongest winds blow. On a second flight that day, the weather officer William Jones-Burdick recorded temperatures inside the storm.

Those winds circle the centre. So once the eye has passed a place, the far side of the eyewall strikes with fierce winds again, from the opposite way. Sailors of old took the eye's calm for the end of the storm; forecasters still warn that the worst winds soon return.

Hurricane and typhoon are regional names for one kind of storm, the tropical cyclone: a hurricane in the Atlantic and the eastern and central Pacific, a typhoon in the western Pacific. The name says nothing of strength. When Hurricane John, born off Mexico in 1994, crossed the International Date Line, it became Typhoon John only because it had moved into another part of the ocean. Back east in September, it was a hurricane again.

A slow hurricane's winds churn the sea, mixing its warm surface water with colder water from below, so the storm cools the sea beneath it by a few degrees and leaves a trail of cooler water, a cold wake. Buoys at sea have measured the drop, and forecasters check how deep the warm water goes, not just how warm its surface is. Over cool water or over land, a hurricane weakens for the same reason: it has lost its supply of warm, moist air. On land, rough ground slows its winds too. Dropsondes, instrument packs dropped by parachute from hurricane-hunter planes, radio back the weakening winds.

Forecasters rank hurricanes on a five-step scale drawn up in the early 1970s by the engineer Herbert Saffir and the meteorologist Robert Simpson. Since 2010 it has rated storms by their strongest steady winds alone. So the scale says nothing of the storm surge, the rise of the sea that a hurricane's winds push ashore, which is often the deadliest part of the storm. Surge caused about half the deaths in US Atlantic storms from 1963 to 2012, though in recent US counts freshwater flooding from rain has killed more. Hurricane Ike, only a Category 2 near Texas in 2008, drove in a surge typical of a Category 4 or 5.
